title: Feet toward the Kaaba
hookLine: tradition says that at Mecca, told his feet pointed at God's house, he asked them to turn his feet where God is not

lines: HIS FEET POINT AT THE KAABA.
AS FAR WEST AS THE JOURNEYS GO.
cards: After a long day of travel, a tired man in a traveler's clothes lies down to sleep.
Without thinking about it, he stretches out with his feet pointing toward the Kaaba, the house Muslims face when they pray, from every corner of the earth.
This is Mecca, about as far west as tradition takes Nanak's journeys. In the morning a qazi, a religious judge, finds him there.
And he's upset, for a reason anyone can understand: to point your feet at something is, in that culture as in Nanak's own, a sign of disrespect.

teach.h: TURN MY FEET WHERE GOD IS NOT.
teach.b: The qazi wakes him roughly. How dare you point your feet at the house of God? And Nanak, tradition says, answers without any anger at all.
Then please, turn my feet toward the direction where God is not.

teach.h: BHAI GURDAS TELLS IT IN HIS VERSES.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas, an early Sikh poet, tells it in his verses, with a wonder: when the qazi dragged Nanak by the feet, Mecca itself turned with them. Miracle or picture, the question is the heart of it. Which way is God not?
What makes the story generous rather than rude is that the qazi's own tradition already agrees with the answer.
Muslims face the Kaaba to pray as one community, in one direction; they don't say God lives inside a building.

teach.h: WHEREVER YOU TURN, THE FACE OF GOD.
teach.b: The Qur'an itself says that the east and the west both belong to God, and that wherever you turn, there is the face of God. So the story isn't a Sikh scoring a point off Islam.

Sikhs tell it as Nanak reminding a pious man of something his own faith already held, the way a friend might remind you of your own best idea. And for Sikhs it echoes the very first symbol of their scripture.
If there is one, and the one is in everything, then no direction you point your feet is empty of God.
Not east, not west, not down. Every direction is full.

how: Sikhs tell the Mecca sakhi, recorded by Bhai Gurdas in his first Var, as a teaching that God is present in every direction; it is often told alongside the Hardwar story as a pair.

o: the place where Muslims believe God lives
the house in Mecca that Muslims face to pray
the mosque in Medina where the Prophet lies

s: Muslims teach that God lives inside the Kaaba
they face it to pray together; the Qur'an says wherever you turn, there is the face of God.
the story is told in Bhai Gurdas's verses
he tells it in his first Var, Mecca turning and all.
in the story, Nanak answers the qazi angrily
he answers calmly, with a question.

games.q: you're a tired traveler in Mecca. a judge wakes you, angry that your feet point at the house of God. what do you say?
o: ask him to turn your feet where God is not.
argue that the building is only stone.
games.why: tradition says Nanak asked him, calmly, to turn his feet toward wherever God is not. there was no such direction.

practice: Stand if you can, face one way, and take a breath, noticing what's in front of you, even if it's a wall; then turn a quarter and breathe again, until you've faced all four.
If you believe in God, you can ask with each turn: is God here too? If you don't, notice that every direction has something in it worth seeing.

wordCard.voice: Kaaba. The house in Mecca that Muslims face to pray, toward which Guru Nanak was asked to turn his feet, and which he asked God was not.
